scenes.title: The problem: a NOC drowning in KPIs while NPS bleeds
scenes.subtitle: The Network Operations Center team drowns in thousands of KPIs across PNFs, VNFs and CNFs — AMF, SMF, UPF and others. When a registration storm or resource exhaustion hits, the signal is buried, the runbook lives in another system, and every second of confusion makes Net Promoter Score plummet and drives customer churn. We want an assistant that behaves like a senior NOC engineer — on call, instantly.
scenes.say: Let's start with the problem, and with what it costs. A network operations center team drowns in thousands of K P I s across physical, virtual and cloud-native network functions — the A M F, the S M F, the U P F, and dozens more. When a registration storm or resource exhaustion hits, the warning signal is buried in that flood, the relevant runbook lives in a different system, and every second of confusion drags the Net Promoter Score down and drives customer churn. What we want is an assistant that behaves like a senior network operations engineer: it inspects the live network state, detects the anomaly, consults the correct runbook, and answers — instantly, and on call. This is course one-oh-one, and this is how we build it on Red Hat OpenShift A I.

scenes.title: Inside the machine: three loops, one platform
scenes.subtitle: Build the truth: telemetry → Feast → Isolation Forest → Model Registry. Use the truth: the agent reads the online store, reasons, and traces every step. Act on the truth: runbook-guided advice a human executes. Full diagrams in the course manual.
scenes.say: Before we walk the dashboard, hold this map in your head — three loops on one platform. Loop one builds the truth: network telemetry is engineered into a Feast feature store, trains an isolation forest, and lands as a versioned model in the registry. Loop two uses the truth: the agent reads the freshest vectors from the online store, reasons with the model and the language model, and traces every step to M L flow. Loop three acts on the truth: a runbook-guided recommendation that a human executes. Each course adds one return-on-investment opportunity on this same platform — and the course manual draws every loop.

scenes.tab: Solution shape — agent as a workload, platform as the backbone
scenes.caption: The agent pod carries only the loop, its MCP skill servers, and runbooks. Everything stateful — features, the model, traces — lives behind platform services it consumes.
scenes.say: Here is the shape of the solution. The agent itself is deliberately small — a disposable, C P U-only pod that carries just the reasoning loop, two skill servers exposed over M C P, and the runbooks. It is agent-as-a-workload. Everything that matters and must persist lives behind platform services the pod merely consumes: the live network state comes from a Feast feature store, the reasoning from a v L L M model endpoint, and every step is traced to M L flow. The classic data-science pipeline that keeps those services truthful — feature engineering, training, scoring — is not hidden in a notebook anymore. It is the platform's job, and the OpenShift A I dashboard shows every stage. Let's walk those stages, because the agent is only as good as the pipeline feeding it.

scenes.tab: Develop & train · Feature store (Feast) — feature views
scenes.caption: One feature view per network function; one noc_telemetry feature service. The pipeline engineers 1-hour rolling mean/min/max per KPI and pushes the latest vector online.
scenes.say: First, features. Our ingest job pulls the real five-G core dataset, engineers one-hour rolling mean, minimum and maximum for each K P I, lands the offline history as parquet, and pushes the latest vector per network function into the online store. On this Feature Store tab you can see the result on our reference cluster, Venice: one feature view per network function, gathered under a single noc-telemetry feature service. This is what gives the agent a truthful, low-latency view of the network — the same features used to train the model are the ones served at inference, so there is no training-serving skew by construction.

scenes.tab: Develop & train · Feature store — data sources
scenes.caption: The offline parquet is a first-class, versioned data source — the point-in-time training set the model learns from.
scenes.say: Feast also registers the offline data source you see here. This matters because it makes the training set reproducible and point-in-time correct. When we train, we retrieve features as they were at the moment of each labeled event — not as they look now. That single discipline is the difference between a demo model and one you would actually trust to flag an incident in production.

scenes.caption: Training is an experiment, not a script. An Isolation Forest per NF, validated against labeled alert windows, every run tracked in MLflow.
scenes.say: Now for training, as a tracked experiment. Our training job retrieves those point-in-time features and fits an anomaly detector — an Isolation Forest — one per network function, then validates it against the labeled alert windows the incident feed provides. On the Experiments tab, every run is captured in M L flow with its parameters, metrics and lineage. Nothing is buried in a notebook on someone's laptop; the whole team sees exactly how each candidate model was produced.

scenes.tab: Develop & train · Model registry — versioned model
scenes.caption: The run logs one pyfunc model that routes each row to its NF's forest, registered as 5gprod-anomaly-isolationforest with full lineage.
scenes.say: Then the model itself: a versioned model, not a pickle in a bucket. The winning run logs a single model that routes each incoming row to the right network function's forest, and registers it under a proper name — five-G-prod anomaly isolation forest. Its lineage — the dataset, the feature source, the window, the train-test split — is all recorded in the parameters you see here. When the agent asks 'is this anomalous', it is calling a specific, auditable version of this model, and we can always answer 'which one, and how was it trained'.

scenes.caption: Promotion is an explicit, governed lifecycle step in the registry — the same mechanism that carried this course unchanged from the Rome cluster to Venice.
scenes.say: And promotion between versions is an explicit, governed step in the registry, shown here. This is the lifecycle control that lets us move a model from candidate to the version the agent actually consumes — deliberately, with a record of who and when. It is also exactly the mechanism that let us stand this whole course up again, unchanged, when we moved from the Rome cluster to Venice.

scenes.caption: Every agent run lands as a full MLflow trace — the question, every tool call, tokens, latency — in the 101-noc-assistant experiment.
scenes.say: And traced reasoning. Every run of the assistant lands here as a full trace: the question it was asked, every tool call it made, the tokens it spent, and how long each step took. Three runs, three traces, each one openable turn by turn. This is the point most teams miss: the agent loop deserves the same observability as any production service. When the assistant says the A M F is anomalous, you open the trace and see exactly which feature read and which scoring call produced that verdict.

scenes.tab: Observe & monitor · Workload metrics — agent as a platform citizen
scenes.caption: The agent and its pipeline jobs run as ordinary, observable OpenShift workloads — CPU-only, restricted-security, disposable.
scenes.say: Finally, the agent and its pipeline jobs are ordinary, observable OpenShift workloads, shown on the workload-metrics tab. C P U-only, restricted security posture, no secrets baked in, disposable. This is the payoff of agent-as-a-workload: the intelligence is a citizen of the platform, monitored and scheduled like anything else, while the heavy, stateful capabilities stay behind services.

scenes.title: 101, solved: classic ML finds it, the agent reasons over it
scenes.subtitle: Isolation Forest finds the anomaly, the alert feed scopes the incident, the language model reasons over both and answers — every step traced. The 'hello world' of agentic telco AI, already doing real work. Next: 201 turns this single assistant into a multi-step RCA investigator. Replay every step yourself in the self-service interactive lab — a time-snapshotted capture of this same cluster — linked from the course page.
scenes.say: So that's one-oh-one, solved end to end on our reference cluster, Venice. The classic model finds the anomaly, the alert feed scopes the incident, and the language model reasons over both before it answers — with every step, classical and generative, traced in one place. It is the hello-world of agentic telco A I, but it already does real work, and every piece is a first-class platform citizen rather than a notebook cell. From here, course two-oh-one turns this single assistant into a multi-step root-cause investigator. Thanks for watching. And you do not have to take this video's word for any of it: the course page links a self-service interactive lab, a time-snapshotted replay of this very cluster, where you run every step and verify every value yourself.
